video_title: Lawfare Daily: The National Guard in Washington, D.C.
gist: Reuters reporter Brad Heath walks Lawfare's Natalie Orpett through his review of ~17,000 DC Superior Court charging documents, finding the National Guard appeared in only 1.3% of criminal matters (217 cases) in the year since deployment, mostly for petty offenses, and that troops are concentrated in wealthier, safer census tracts while the tracts they avoid account for 82% of DC murders. The conversation quantifies the fiscal cost (an administration ask of ~$1.5 billion to sustain the deployment through the end of Trump's second term), the opportunity cost to source cities, and the near-total opacity around command, mission authority, and coordination with local police.

insights.claim: A review of roughly 17,000 publicly available DC Superior Court charging documents covering the year after National Guard troops arrived in Washington found the Guard appeared in any capacity in just 1.3% of criminal matters, or 217 cases.
insights.speaker: Brad Heath, Reuters reporter
insights.so_what: The signature federal 'get tough on crime' deployment produces almost no measurable law-enforcement output, which weakens the factual predicate defenders will need if courts or Congress scrutinize the mission or its funding.
insights.quote: The National Guard made an appearance in one form or another in 1.3% of the criminal matters that were handled in DC in the year since they arrived.

insights.claim: About half of the 217 DC cases involving National Guard troops were soldiers acting like police, but the underlying offenses were overwhelmingly petty: subway fare-gate jumping, a shoplifter who took roughly $7 of Slim Jims from a CVS, and a woman who drank an unpaid-for 20-ounce root beer at a 7-Eleven.
insights.speaker: Brad Heath, Reuters reporter
insights.so_what: The mismatch between military deployment cost and the triviality of resulting cases is the clearest ammunition for critics arguing the mission is symbolic rather than functional.
insights.quote: there was one fairly recently where a guy stole two slim gyms, like the the beef jerky sticks from a CVS. They're worth about $7 and and soldiers stopped him.

insights.claim: In roughly 30 of the DC cases the National Guard appeared only as witnesses who reported what they saw to police rather than intervening, a role indistinguishable from any ordinary bystander in a charging document.
insights.speaker: Brad Heath, Reuters reporter
insights.so_what: If most Guard 'involvement' is passive witnessing, claims of operational value rest on deterrence rather than enforcement, and deterrence is the one claim the data cannot support.
insights.quote: there there's I think 30 odd cases like that where where in one way or another or another they've provided information to the police but didn't actually like lay hands on somebody.

insights.claim: The lead case in the Reuters investigation was a violent assault outside a DC nightclub in which the responding officer's report noted that 15 National Guard members were on patrol in the area and did nothing at all, directly undercutting the deterrence rationale for the deployment.
insights.speaker: Brad Heath, Reuters reporter
insights.so_what: A documented instance of armed troops present at a violent crime and not intervening is the kind of specific fact that reframes the policy debate from legality to efficacy.
insights.quote: he makes a point of noting that there were 15 National Guard members on patrol in the area who didn't do anything at all.

insights.claim: A surprisingly large share of the DC cases involving National Guard members had soldiers as the crime victims, including nine counted incidents of being spat on, and those are prosecuted as assault on a police officer because most deployed soldiers are deputized as US marshals.
insights.speaker: Brad Heath, Reuters reporter
insights.so_what: Marshal deputization quietly converts soldiers into federal law enforcement for charging purposes, escalating ordinary street friction into federal-grade offenses and expanding the deployment's legal footprint beyond what the mission statements describe.
insights.quote: if not all of the soldiers on the street, at least a large number of them are deputized as US marshals. Uh so so to spit on them is to spit on a police officer, which is a more serious charge than spitting on you or me.

insights.claim: Two National Guard soldiers were themselves charged with crimes for off-duty weapons possession in DC, and both cases were dismissed quickly by the US attorney's office.
insights.speaker: Brad Heath, Reuters reporter
insights.so_what: Differential charging treatment for deployed soldiers is a latent accountability story that could surface in litigation or oversight hearings.
insights.quote: There there were two where soldiers were charged with crimes for offduty weapons possession. Uh both of those got pretty quickly dismissed by the US attorney's office.

insights.claim: The DC National Guard deployment scaled from an initial 800 troops to north of 4,600 at its summer peak and has since drawn down to roughly 3,600, with weekly official updates now disclosing headcount and home states.
insights.speaker: Brad Heath, Reuters reporter
insights.so_what: The drawdown trajectory is the leading indicator for whether the multi-billion-dollar sustainment request actually gets spent or quietly shrinks.
insights.quote: Now I think we're down to 3600. So it seems like the the summer deployment is winding down some.

insights.claim: Mapping the census tracts where National Guard troops generated court-documented incidents showed they concentrate in wealthier, whiter, and already-safer parts of DC, while the tracts where they were absent account for 82% of the city's murders.
insights.speaker: Brad Heath, Reuters reporter
insights.so_what: Deployment geography, not force size, is the decisive fact: troops are stationed where violent crime is not, which makes any claimed crime effect statistically implausible.
insights.quote: the census tracks where they were not is where 82% of the DC murders happen

insights.claim: Violent crime is falling by comparable amounts in DC neighborhoods with and without National Guard presence, and Baltimore is hitting record-low homicides despite having federal resources pulled away to staff the DC surge, which makes the deterrence claim empirically unprovable.
insights.speaker: Brad Heath, Reuters reporter
insights.so_what: A control city that lost federal resources and still hit record lows destroys the causal story politicians are selling, and national homicide lows mean any city can claim credit for a trend it did not create.
insights.quote: Baltimore, which has not had a a federal surge and in some sense has had like federal resources withdrawn from the city to bring them to DC, is also experiencing kind of record low homicides

insights.claim: Total violent crimes reported to DC's Metropolitan Police are actually a couple of percentage points higher this year than last, driven mostly by serious assaults, even as homicide numbers decline during the federal surge.
insights.speaker: Brad Heath, Reuters reporter
insights.so_what: The headline 'crime is down' framing depends entirely on which series you cite; the assault series cuts the other way and is available to whichever side wants it.
insights.quote: if you look at just like the total number of violent crimes reported to Metropolitan Police, it's actually higher this year than it was last year.

insights.claim: The administration has most recently said it needs close to $1.5 billion to keep National Guard soldiers in Washington DC through the end of President Trump's second term.
insights.speaker: Brad Heath, Reuters reporter
insights.so_what: A concrete, multi-year appropriations number gives Congress a discrete line item to fight over and makes the deployment's duration a budget question rather than only a legal one.
insights.quote: The administration most recently said, you know, they need close to $1.5 billion dollars to keep soldiers in DC through the end of President Trump's second term.

insights.claim: The deployed National Guard force considerably outnumbers DC's sworn police officers and costs considerably more per day than the entire Metropolitan Police Department, in a city that was already the most heavily policed large city in the United States before counting Capitol Police, Park Police, and the Secret Service.
insights.speaker: Brad Heath, Reuters reporter
insights.so_what: Framing the spend as an alternative to permanent, locally accountable police hiring is the most potent fiscal critique and the one DC officials have hinted at.
insights.quote: these soldiers outnumber the sworn officers on DC's police department like considerably. and they cost more than DC's police department considerably on a daily basis.

insights.claim: One identified soldier guarding a DC Metro station turned out to be a decorated police officer from Jackson, Mississippi, a city with a far worse per-capita homicide problem and far fewer officers than DC, illustrating that the deployment drains policing capacity from more dangerous cities.
insights.speaker: Brad Heath, Reuters reporter
insights.so_what: The unmeasured cost is policing capacity subtracted from high-violence cities elsewhere, an argument that could peel off support from law-and-order constituencies in those states.
insights.quote: one of the costs to the deployment was they had to take a, you know, an officer out of a a quite dangerous US city to have them guard the subway.

insights.claim: A Louisiana police chief who welcomed the idea of National Guard troops on his streets realized the call-up would pull his own officers away, because many local police also serve in National Guard military police units.
insights.speaker: Brad Heath, Reuters reporter
insights.so_what: Guard deployments are partly a reshuffling of the same police manpower, so any city requesting troops should model the offsetting loss of its own force.
insights.quote: if you call up the National Guard, that's going to be a bunch of my officers because they also are National Guard, you know, soldiers in a military police unit.

insights.claim: None of the DC charging documents reviewed disclose whether the National Guard members involved were operating under Title 10, Title 32, or state active duty status, which are precisely the facts that determine whether their law enforcement activity is lawful.
insights.speaker: Brad Heath, Reuters reporter
insights.so_what: The record that would settle the legality question simply does not exist in the public case files, which pushes resolution into discovery and prolongs the legal uncertainty overhanging the deployment.

insights.claim: Defense counsel for anyone detained or arrested by a National Guard member has a live unlawful-arrest motion available, because the scope of Guard authority to arrest versus merely detain is contested and fact-specific, and body-camera footage and paperwork produced even in petty cases could surface command-and-control facts.
insights.speaker: Natalie Orpett, Lawfare executive editor
insights.so_what: Routine misdemeanor discovery is a plausible back door into facts about the deployment's legal architecture that no agency will volunteer.
insights.quote: if I were a defense lawyer and my client had been detained or arrested by a member of the National Guard, I would have motions relating to unlawful arrest

insights.claim: The two stated DC missions have been conflated in practice, with Governor Whitmer recalling Michigan's National Guard contribution after concluding troops sent for the America 250 crowd-control mission were being used for the broader DC Safe and Beautiful crime mission.
insights.speaker: Natalie Orpett, Lawfare executive editor
insights.so_what: Governors withdrawing troops over mission creep is the practical constraint on deployment size, and it operates faster than litigation.

insights.claim: The states supplying National Guard troops to DC number around twenty and are principally but not exclusively states with Republican governors, with some states contributing as little as a single person.
insights.speaker: Brad Heath, Reuters reporter
insights.so_what: Token single-soldier contributions suggest political signaling rather than operational need, and the partisan skew makes the force composition vulnerable to state-level politics.
insights.quote: They are principally but not exclusively uh states with Republican governors.

insights.claim: Basic operational facts about the DC deployment, including who issues daily orders, what training soldiers receive before patrolling, and which units are present, remain unanswered because the National Guard declined interviews, DC government declined to comment, and soldiers are barred from speaking to press.
insights.speaker: Brad Heath, Reuters reporter
insights.so_what: Sustained opacity around a highly visible domestic military deployment is itself the rule-of-law story, and FOIA timelines mean documentary answers may not arrive for a decade.
insights.quote: the extent to which we still don't really know like who tells you where to go every day, who gives you your marching orders, what exactly is the training regimen that you have to have before you come and are on the streets of DC

themes.theme: DC Home Rule and Local Politics

insights.claim: DC government officials were markedly more reluctant to discuss the National Guard deployment than they have been on other federal-local friction points, because the city must manage its relationship with federal authority from a position of structural weakness under limited home rule.
insights.speaker: Brad Heath, Reuters reporter
insights.so_what: Local silence means the factual record on domestic deployments will be built by journalists and litigants rather than by the affected city government.
insights.quote: the the number of people in DC government who like declined to talk about this at all was was surprising to me.

insights.claim: Mayor Bowser drew a distinction in accepting hundreds of additional federal agents acting as local police during the 2025 anti-crime surge while opposing both ICE and the National Guard in DC.
insights.speaker: Brad Heath, Reuters reporter
insights.so_what: The line local leaders will actually defend is military and immigration enforcement, not federal law enforcement generally, which shapes where future federal-local conflicts detonate.

insights.claim: The Metropolitan Police Department is not working alongside the National Guard but merely responding when called, and DC appears to have little or no control over where soldiers are posted or what they do.
insights.speaker: Brad Heath, Reuters reporter
insights.so_what: Without coordination, the claimed benefit that troops free up local police for other work has no evidentiary support and should not be assumed in any cost-benefit assessment.
insights.quote: they don't really have much control over where the soldiers go or what the soldiers do.

insights.claim: Residents of DC's highest-crime neighborhoods showed little appetite for having National Guard troops redeployed to their areas, saying what the community needs is trusted community policing and crime-solving rather than a rotating cast of armed soldiers.
insights.speaker: Brad Heath, Reuters reporter
insights.so_what: There is no constituency asking for the troops in the places the policy nominally targets, which limits any political upside from expanding the mission's geography.
insights.quote: if they're here to nominally make the city safer, would you like them to be in the parts of the city that are less safe? And I did not get a lot of enthusiasm in response to that proposition.

insights.claim: DC crime statistics themselves are contested, with the DC Inspector General finding shortcomings in how the Metropolitan Police handle crime reporting, commanders being ousted, and a separate investigation finding pressure to suppress serious crime numbers in areas targeted by policing initiatives.
insights.speaker: Brad Heath, Reuters reporter
insights.so_what: Every side of this debate is arguing from the same questionable dataset, so any analysis resting on DC crime statistics carries unpriced measurement risk.
insights.quote: are our data any good? It's tricky to know. I mean, the White House uses them, the district uses them, the FBI uses them. So, they they're what you got.

insights.claim: The federal anti-crime surge in DC coincided immediately with a notable decline in public mobility, with fewer bike-share and taxi trips and fewer restaurant reservations, an economic side effect distinct from any crime outcome.
insights.speaker: Brad Heath, Reuters reporter
insights.so_what: Mobility and reservation data are real-time, publicly observable proxies for the local commercial cost of militarized enforcement in any city that gets a similar surge.
insights.quote: there was a pretty notable decrease in public mobility, right? Like fewer people were taking the the bike shares and taxis and just le fewer people on the street making restaurant reservations.

insights.claim: General Randy Manor, former second in command of the National Guard Bureau, argued that soldiers are ill-prepared for police work because their training is combat-oriented rather than community-oriented, and that stationing them to watch American civilians risks permanently changing how communities perceive a force they previously associated with disaster relief.
insights.speaker: Brad Heath, Reuters reporter (quoting Gen. Randy Manor)
insights.so_what: Erosion of the Guard's disaster-relief goodwill is a long-duration institutional cost that outlasts any single administration's deployment decision.
insights.quote: now you have the National Guard on the streets of a US city kind of keeping an eye on you. Now, you know, they they might be protecting you for crime, but they might also be checking you out to make sure you are not committing any crime.

insights.claim: Some DC residents and officials treat the National Guard standing idle near the National Mall, the White House, and Metro stations as a preferable outcome to active enforcement, because expanded Guard activity creates more opportunities for incidents to escalate.
insights.speaker: Brad Heath, Reuters reporter
insights.so_what: The political economy is inverted: low operational output is the local success condition, which means pressure to 'do more' would raise, not lower, tail risk of a violent incident.
insights.quote: having the National Guard standing around the mall near the White House at metro stations and not really doing anything is a pretty important victory
